analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal long-term care insurance benefit for retired Americans with serious disabilities.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill creating a federal long-term care benefit, backed by five cosponsors from both parties, has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee since its March 2025 introduction without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The WISH Act would add a new benefit to Social Security for older Americans who develop serious long-term disabilities, such as being unable to bathe or dress without help. After a waiting period of one to five years depending on lifetime income, the government would pay a monthly cash benefit worth about six hours a day of paid home care, scaled to the person's work history. The goal is to protect middle-class families from spending down their savings and ending up on Medicaid, and to leave the first stretch of care to personal savings and private insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired Americans who develop serious long-term disabilities, especially middle-class families who would otherwise exhaust their savings to pay for care and then qualify for Medicaid. The bill's own findings say more than half of people entering old age will need long-term care at an average cost of $298,000, and that 1 in 5 middle-income seniors will end up impoverished and on Medicaid. Family members who provide unpaid care would also benefit, since the benefit can pay for hired help.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older Americans facing catastrophic care costs

how_it_helps.text: The bill covers only the catastrophic tail of long-term care: a monthly cash benefit equal to the median cost of six hours a day of paid personal assistance, payable for as long as the serious disability lasts, so a multi-year care need would no longer wipe out a family's nest egg.

The waiting period before benefits start is 12 months for people at or below the 40th percentile of lifetime earnings and grows longer for higher earners, up to five years, targeting protection at people least able to self-insure.

Benefit payments would not count as income or an asset for any federal, state, or locally financed program, so recipients would not lose other benefits like Medicaid or food assistance because of the payments.

The benefit amount is indexed to wages in the long-term care workforce, and recipients who hire non-family caregivers must pay minimum wage and withhold payroll taxes, which supports the paid care workforce.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill creates a new Federal Long-Term Care Insurance Trust Fund seeded with $12 million a year for fiscal 2026-2028 plus $50 million for public education, but it includes no dedicated tax or payroll contribution, so ongoing benefit costs would depend on future appropriations. People with private savings would still bear the full cost of care during the one-to-five-year waiting period.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and families during the waiting period

drawbacks.text: The bill covers nothing for the first 12 months of a serious disability for lower earners, and up to five years for the highest earners, leaving families fully exposed during the initial and often most disruptive period of care; the bill explicitly intends that early period to be covered by personal responsibility and private insurance.

People who are disabled before retirement age, or who lack enough work quarters to be insured, get nothing under this bill; the bill itself requires HHS to report on the unmet needs of those excluded groups, including people disabled in childhood.

The startup funding is tiny relative to the benefit's potential cost, and the trust fund relies only on gifts, bequests, and annual appropriations with no dedicated revenue stream, so the program's long-term financing would have to be settled in separate legislation.
The benefit is scaled to work history (6 quarters required for insured status, full benefit at 40 quarters), so people with thin or interrupted work records receive proportionally small benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The catastrophic-only design is a genuine strength: it targets the risk that impoverishes nearly all households, keeps the federal cost manageable, and pushes people to plan for shorter care spells. But the same design means families remain fully on the hook during the first year or more of care, often when they are least equipped to cope, and the bill offers no answer for who pays beyond modest startup appropriations. It is a real but partial fix, and its fate would depend entirely on future Congresses funding it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2025 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it; with Congress still in session, it is waiting for a hearing or markup that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Suozzi (D-NY) introduced the bill on March 11, 2025, together with Representative John Moolenaar (R-MI), and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill has five cosponsors: three Republicans and two Democrats, making it bipartisan from the start.
No further legislative action, hearing, or vote appears in the bill's action history since the referral.

The bill cites HHS data that more than half of Americans entering old age will have a long-term care need averaging $298,000 over about two years of serious disability, that only 11% of adults have any private long-term care coverage, and that 1 in 5 middle-income seniors will end up impoverished and dependent on Medicaid.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. The bill has not advanced past committee, so the current system, in which families pay out of pocket until they are poor enough to qualify for Medicaid, continues unchanged, and private long-term care insurers and Medicaid-funded nursing homes face no new competition from a public benefit.

for.name: Thomas Suozzi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan cosponsors

for.name: John Moolenaar
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as the named Republican cosponsor

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 11, 2025; the committee has taken no further action, holding the bill without a hearing or markup

sides.party_line_note: Support is split across both parties at introduction: the sponsor is a Democrat, the named original cosponsor is a Republican, and the five cosponsors include three Republicans and two Democrats; no one has opposed it on the record, though the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee has not moved it.

industries.note: The bill's design deliberately leaves the first years of care to personal savings and private coverage, and directs $50 million to a public education campaign telling Americans to consider private insurance alongside family support, making private insurers the expected channel for early-period care while the new public benefit backstops the catastrophic tail. Only about 11% of adults currently have any private long-term care coverage, so the public plan would both create a backstop that reduces demand for private policies and use public money to promote them.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and direct-care workers
industries.note: A monthly benefit worth six hours a day of paid assistance, indexed to care-sector wages, would create a large new funding stream for paid home care. The bill also requires beneficiaries who hire non-family caregivers to comply with minimum wage and payroll tax withholding laws.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and Medicaid long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill's stated purpose is to reduce what it calls necessary reliance on Medicaid, and families protected from spend-down would be less likely to enter nursing homes as impoverished Medicaid patients. But the cash benefit could also be used to pay for facility care, so the impact is not clearly negative for the industry.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the early markers of a bill that stalls: a first-term referral to Ways and Means, no hearing or markup scheduled, and a small bipartisan cosponsor list. Long-term care insurance programs have a difficult history in Congress, and this bill's long-term financing is unresolved, which committees typically want settled before action. It could pick up cosponsors, but floor action this Congress would require both committee interest and a funding deal that the bill does not yet contain.
